summary: Provides a framework for IP fast-reroute mechanisms that protect against link or router failure by using repair paths decided locally. Unlike MPLS fast-reroute, it works with conventional IP routing and forwarding. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If a bridge closes, a driver with a backup route already in mind can turn immediately instead of waiting for news. This document describes how routers can have such backup routes ready.

questions: how do routers recover quickly from link failure
what is a loop free alternate
what is a micro loop in routing
subtitle: A framework for routers to switch to pre-computed backup paths the moment a link or neighbor fails, without waiting for the network to reconverge.

tldr.problem: When a link or router fails, traffic is disrupted until the whole network re-converges, which has traditionally taken at least several seconds and is still too slow for emerging sensitive services.
tldr.mechanism: Routers adjacent to a failure use locally determined repair paths computed in advance (equal-cost paths, loop-free alternates or multi-hop paths), plus optional micro-loop prevention, without first telling other routers.
tldr.outcome: This is a framework, not a protocol: it sets scope, terminology and the sub-problems that concrete IPFRR solutions must address.

today: RFC 5714 is an Informational framework, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Concrete mechanisms are left to other documents, such as the loop-free alternates specification in RFC 5286.

sections.title: The Problem with Slow Reconvergence
sections.content:
After a link or node failure, packets for destinations reached through the failed component may be dropped or may loop until the network re-converges. Traditionally this lasted at least several seconds. Recent router advances brought it under a second for carefully configured link state IGP networks, but new services may be sensitive to losses orders of magnitude shorter, and the distributed nature of the network limits how fast convergence can be.

IP fast-reroute (IPFRR) takes another approach: compute backup routes so the router detecting the failure repairs it locally, without immediately informing other routers. Disruption is then limited to the time to detect the adjacent failure and invoke the backup. This is analogous to MPLS fast-reroute (RFC 4090), but the mechanisms for pure IP networks are necessarily very different.
sections.eli5: Waiting for every router to hear about a broken road takes ages. It is quicker if the driver at the broken spot already knows the detour.

sections.title: Scope and Where Time Goes
sections.content:
The initial scope is link state IGPs, whose topology information makes repair paths easier to compute. Non-link-state IGPs and BGP are left for further study, although traffic for destinations outside the IGP domain must still be handled correctly. Complete protection against multiple unrelated failures is out of scope.

The RFC breaks a conventional routing transition into five time costs: detecting the failure (milliseconds at the physical layer up to several tens of seconds with routing protocol Hellos), reacting locally, passing news to other routers (typically 10 to 100 milliseconds per hop), recomputing forwarding tables (typically a few milliseconds), and loading the new tables into forwarding hardware (possibly several hundred milliseconds). Differences in the last step are a main cause of micro-loops.
sections.eli5: Fixing a broken road involves noticing it, telling everyone, redrawing maps and printing new copies. The slowest and most uneven part is printing the maps.

sections.title: Detection and Repair Paths
sections.content:
Fast failure detection can use physical detection such as loss of light, a routing-protocol-independent protocol such as BFD, or routing protocol fast Hellos. Packet-based detection needs care about false failure indications, which can be reduced by prioritizing the detection packets.

Repair paths should be pre-calculated for each local failure. Three basic categories exist:

  • Equal cost multi-paths (ECMP): alternate paths that do not use the failure can trivially serve as repairs.
  • Loop-free alternates: a direct neighbor has a path to the destination that is guaranteed not to traverse the failure (see RFC 5286).
  • Multi-hop repair paths: a router more than one hop away forwards traffic to the destination without crossing the failure.

The RFC anticipates that around 80% of failures can be repaired with ECMP and loop-free alternates alone, and around 98% with repair paths reaching two hops away, but notes such figures are illustrative and may not always be achievable.
sections.eli5: A backup can be another equally good road, a neighbor's road that does not lead back to you, or a longer detour through a faraway town.

sections.title: Multi-Hop Repairs, Coverage and Maintenance
sections.content:
Multi-hop repairs fall into three families: pre-computed alternate FIBs selected by per-packet signaling (such as U-turn detection or packet marking), mechanisms equivalent to a loose source route such as tunnels, and special addresses or labels installed in all routers, such as not-via addresses.

Repair coverage can be measured four ways: the percentage of links or nodes fully protected, the percentage of destinations protected for all failures, the percentage of all destination and failure combinations protected, or the percentage of normal packets that still arrive. Link protection is generally simpler than node protection, and a node-protecting repair also covers link failure except where the adjacent node is a single point of failure.

Repair paths and their FIB entries are expected, though not required, to be pre-computed and installed. They stay in force until the routing protocol has re-converged, and they can then be recomputed as a background task, subject to a hold-down. Repaired traffic may congest links, so ways to spread it are desirable. LAN protection is more complex than point-to-point.
sections.eli5: Backup plans can be measured by how many roads, towns or trips they cover. After the maps are fixed, the router quietly redraws its backup plans for the next time.

sections.title: Micro-Loops and Management
sections.content:
Micro-loops can drop traffic and, by saturating a link with looping packets, cause congestion that discards otherwise unaffected traffic (RFC 5715 summarizes solutions). Repair paths without micro-loop control may be starved of traffic, while micro-loop control without repair paths means traffic is discarded at the failure. Micro-loops can also arise when a link or node is restored.

Management should cover enabling or disabling IPFRR, per-link or per-node protection, repair path preferences, failure detection and loop-avoidance configuration. Monitoring should report what cannot be protected, the pre-computed repair paths, counts of detections, invocations and repaired packets, and support testing repairs.
sections.eli5: When routers disagree about the map for a moment, cars can circle round and round. The framework asks for ways to stop that and for tools to see how the backups are doing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework introduces no security issues itself, but proposed solutions need scrutiny. If tunnels are used, they must not become an attack vector; one method is to use tunnel endpoint addresses that user traffic cannot use.

Many solutions make traffic arrive from a direction that fails a standard reverse path forwarding (RPF) check, so a network that relies on RPF for security needs another mechanism. Because repair paths often have a different length, security mechanisms that rely on specific TTL values are also affected.
sections.eli5: Detour roads can confuse the guards who check which way visitors came from, so the guards need new rules.

viz.caption: THE THREE BASIC KINDS OF REPAIR PATH

items.title: ECMP
items.text: Another equal-cost path that avoids the failure.

items.title: Loop-free alternate
items.text: A direct neighbor whose path to the destination does not cross the failure.

items.title: Multi-hop repair
items.text: A router more than one hop away from which traffic reaches the destination safely.
